meta.title: Neural Playground · {brand}
meta.description: An interactive replay of open monkey motor-cortex recordings, decoded into a cursor path on reaches the decoder never saw. Research demo; not a medical device; no hardware is controlled.

hero.heading: Neural Playground
hero.lede: Replay spikes recorded from neurons in a monkey's motor cortex while it reached for targets, and watch a simple decoder turn them into a cursor path. Every trace and score on this page comes from reaches the decoder never saw while it was being fitted.

banner: Research demo on open monkey motor-cortex data. Not a medical device. Offline replay of a past recording; no hardware is controlled.

raster.caption: Each row is one neuron and each tick one spike. Faded rows are neurons the decoder does not use at this setting; tinted ticks are the added noise. The line marks the replay time.
raster.label: Spike raster of the selected trial

score.heading: How close is the decoded path?
score.testSet: R² of decoded position, all held-out test reaches
score.velocity: R² of decoded velocity, all held-out test reaches
score.trial: Average gap between decoded and actual cursor, this trial only
score.explain: R² is the share of the variation in the actual movement that the decoded movement accounts for. One is a perfect match; zero is no better than always guessing the average. A single short reach is judged by its average gap instead, because R² over one reach swings widely.
score.chartCaption: Test-set R² of decoded position for both decoders at the current noise setting. Lines show the average over several random subsets of neurons and shaded bands their range; the dot marks the setting shown above.
score.chartLabel: Line chart of decoding accuracy against the number of neurons used

steps.heading: Record
steps.body: A grid of electrodes in the motor cortex picked up spikes from individual neurons while a monkey moved its hand to steer a cursor to targets that appeared one after another.

steps.heading: Count
steps.body: Spikes are counted in short time bins: one count per neuron per bin. That table of counts is all the decoder sees.

steps.heading: Fit
steps.body: A linear decoder learns how the counts relate to cursor position and velocity, using training reaches only. The ridge filter weighs the last half second of counts; the Kalman filter also assumes the cursor moves smoothly.

steps.heading: Test
steps.body: The fitted decoder then runs on reaches it never saw. Those decoded paths and their scores are what this page shows.

limits.heading: What this demo does not show
items: It is an offline replay of one recording session from one monkey. Nothing is decoded in real time, and no human brain data is used.
The decoders were fitted and tested within the same session. Implanted electrodes drift across days and months, which this demo does not model.
The added noise is random extra spikes, a simple stand-in for recording noise, not a model of any particular device.
The arm is a drawing. It is not connected to a robot, a prosthesis or any other hardware.
It is not a medical device and says nothing about anyone's health or thoughts.

data.heading: About the data and method
data.controlText: the same ridge filter fitted to movements shifted by half the session scores a test R² of
data.reproduce: Derived from MC_RTT (CC BY 4.0); changes were made: we excerpted twelve held-out reaches, counted spikes in fifty-millisecond bins, split the reaches into training, validation and test sets, decoded them with linear decoders, rounded positions to a tenth of a millimetre and, when you choose added noise, mixed in simulated random spikes. The dataset's creators do not endorse {brand}. The offline pipeline, the pinned file hash and the random seed are in the repository under tools/playground, so every number on this page can be recomputed from the public file.
